Items.Authors: Yinzi Xin, Nemanja Jovanovic, Dimitri Mawet, Daniel Echeverri, Yoo Jung Kim, Jonathan Lin, Julien Lozi, Sebastien Vievard, Olivier Guyon, Grace Piroscia, Vincent Déo, Sergio Leon-Saval, Rodrigo Amezcua-Correa, Stephanos Yerolatsitis, Michael P. Fitzgerald, Pradip Gatkine, Suvinay Goyal, Barnaby Norris, Garreth Ruane, Steph Sallum
Items.Title: The Photonic Lantern Nuller: from concept to laboratory and on-sky demonstrations
Items.Abstract: This thesis work presents the conceptual design and experimental characterization of the Photonic Lantern Nuller instrument, which uses a multimode-to-single-mode demultiplexing waveguide to cancel out starlight while maintaining planet light, allowing for the direct characterization of planets at a telescope’s diffraction limit. The PLN was experimentally characterized in the lab, where it was further enhanced using common-path wavefront sensing and control techniques, and then demonstrated on sky at the Subaru Telescope. Highlights include measured in-lab null-depths of ~10^{-4} in three out of four ports simultaneously and on-sky null-depths of ~10^{-1} (limited by jitter and atmospheric residuals). We provide an overview of these results and discuss avenues for future work.

Items.Authors: Phillip Black
Items.Title: Introducing L-BASS: an instrument to create absolutely calibrated maps at 1.4 GHz
Items.Abstract: The L-Band All-Sky Survey (L-BASS) is a new ground-based instrument at the Jodrell Bank Observatory designed to deliver an absolutely calibrated all-sky map at 1.4 GHz with ≤ 0.1 K radiometric accuracy and 23° angular resolution. L-BASS combines classic differential radio-astronomy techniques with a modern constant-comparison receiver architecture and digital spectrometer back-end. The telescope employs two identical conical horn antennas, each producing circularly polarised outputs and independently steerable in elevation. L-BASS is calibrated with strategies including, the incorporation of a continuous-wave (CW) calibration technique, injecting a signal for running gain tracking, an array of 1-Wire thermometers for passive loss modelling, meteorological monitoring and an absolute calibration stage using a cryogenic reference load.

Items.Authors: Philippe Dierickx, Gaston Gausachs, Corentin Cudennec, Benoît Sassolas, William Sutherland, Simone D'Auria, Laurane Fréour, Peter Doel, Tony Travouillon, Roland Bacon, Laurent Pinard, Vincenzo Cianniello, Vincenzo De Caprio, Ciro Del Vecchio, Salvatore Savarese, Olga Bellido, Thomas Augusteijn, Ramón Navarro, Will Saunders
Items.Title: Progress of the design of the 12-m optical, Wide-Field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST)
Items.Abstract: The Wide-Field Spectroscopic Telescope (WST) is a 12-m class, Alt-Az optical telescope providing two simultaneously available foci, 2º and 3x3 arc minutes respectively, for Multi-Object Spectroscopy (MOS) and Integral Field Spectroscopy (IFS). We outline the original optical solution, report progress of the structural design, of functional and physical definitions, and of the design of high-performance coatings of the telescope optics. The telescope can be wavefront-controlled at both foci, with little if any crosstalk between MOS and IFS controls. The design provides an option for seeing reduction at the IFS field, within existing technology. With a view to minimising risks, designs build extensively on solutions implemented in ESO’s VLT and ELT programmes. The WST would be located near ESO’s Paranal-Armazones observatory.

Items.Authors: Clémentine Béchet, Éric Thiébaut, Michel Tallon, Isabelle Tallon-Bosc, Bernard Gelly, Richard Douet
Items.Title: Self-calibration of an adaptive optics system and its application to THEMIS solar telescope
Items.Abstract: Since 2021, THEMIS solar telescope (Spain) is equipped with an adaptive optics (AO) system developed by the Airi team at CRAL. This led us to revisit AO calibration in the working conditions of the AO system and with original features. Random probing commands are sent to the deformable mirror in open or close-loop at the AO loop framerate to fit an affine model of the system by weighted least-squares. Equations are analyzed to compare estimates directly from the data to estimates using the difference of two successive data (differential data) which reduces the variance of the nuisance. Differential data methods include widely spread push-pull calibration, although we show that differential data can be used generally without push-pull sequence. In addition, simple updating rules compatible with large AO systems are derived from a generalisation of the Recursive Least Squares. Finally, we review the benefits of this approach from data registered on the Sun with THEMIS.

Items.Authors: Melissa Pesce-Rollins, Hamish Reid, Daniel Ryan, Alexander Warmuth, Samuel Krucker, Philippe Laurent, Olivier Limousin, Jake Mitchell, Albert Y. Shih, Nicole Vilmer, Andrea Battaglia, Shane Maloney, Sophie Musset, Hakan Onel
Items.Title: The Large Area Spectrometer for Solar Accelerated Nuclei (LASSAN): a next-generation solar gamma-ray spectroscopic instrument concept
Items.Abstract: We present the Large Area Spectrometer for Solar Accelerated Nuclei (LASSAN), one of two instruments on the Solar Particle Acceleration Radiation and Kinematics (SPARK) mission, currently in Step 2 of ESA’s M-class Mission Opportunity 2025. LASSAN provides spectroscopy from 40 keV to 100 MeV on ≤10 s timescales and offers over 40 times the effective area of previous instruments such as RHESSI, enabled by high-resolution pixelated gadolinium–aluminum–gallium garnet (GAGG) scintillator detectors. Its large effective area and high spectral resolution will, for the first time, enable routine simultaneous detection of bremsstrahlung, nuclear de-excitation lines, and pion-decay emission on sub-10 s timescales. These measurements will constrain electron and ion spectra, composition, timing, and energy content across hundreds of flares, addressing key open questions on solar particle acceleration and the origins of space-weather disturbances

Items.Authors: Kathleen Harrington, The Simons Observatory Collaboration
Items.Title: The Simons Observatory: on-sky noise performance of the small aperture telescopes
Items.Abstract: The Simons Observatory (SO) is a next generation cosmic microwave background (CMB) experiment now operating in the Chilean Atacama Desert. The initial SO configuration includes three 0.5-meter Small Aperture Telescopes (SATs) that are targeting observations of the larger angular scales of the CMB polarization anisotropy in a search for the B-mode polarization signature that would indicate the presence of inflation-sourced primordial gravitation waves. Each SAT contains over 12,000 transition edge sensor detectors; the two Mid-frequency SATs, observing in bands around 90 and 150 GHz, completed commissioning in the Fall of 2024 and the ultra-high frequency SAT, observing bands around 220 and 280 GHz, began commissioning in the Fall of 2025. I will discuss the efficiency calibrations and noise performance of deployed instruments as well as compare the achieved performance to forecasting and instrument modeling expectations.

Items.Authors: Krittapas Chanchaiworawit, Kantapong Tharawan, That Chomchuen, Jitsupa Paenoi, Thansita Thomrungpiyathan, Pakawat Prasit, Samattachai Tanun, Teerawat Kuha, Auychai Laoyang, Pathompong Butpan, Rungrit Anutarawiramkul, Anuphong Inpan, Suchinno Kanthum, Picha Ruenarrom, Tarathon Intaros, Manlika Pinkaew, Apichat Leckngam
Items.Title: LRS and CoLoRS: the next generation instruments for rapid spectroscopic follow-up for the Thai National Telescope and the Thai Robotic Telescopes Network
Items.Abstract: NARIT is deploying a new generation of spectrographs on the Thai National Telescope (TNT) and the Thai Robotic Telescope Network (TRTs) to strengthen global time-domain astronomy. The Low Resolution Spectrograph (LRS) on the 2.4-m TNT delivers R≈375–1000 over 400–800 nm in long-slit and slitless modes, reaching surface-brightness limits of SB_r’≈20.5 mag/arcsec² in one hour. While CoLoRS at the TRTs provides rapid R=100–200 spectroscopy with S/N>100 for r’≈12 mag targets, and its forthcoming upgrade, CoLoRS-NEX, adds simultaneous NIR imaging across a ≥10′ field. Together, these systems enable rapid transient classification, exoplanet study, AGN characterization, and sensitive extragalactic surveys, positioning Thailand as a key contributor to next-generation time-domain science.

Items.Authors: Runa Briguglio, Marco Xompero, Giorgio Pariani, Nicolò Azzaroli, Luca Oggioni, Pietro Ferraiuolo, Matteo Menessini, Riccardo Grignaffini, Chiara Scandaglia, Armando Riccardi, Elise Vernet, Aglae Kellerer
Items.Title: Optical calibration of the ELT-M4: automated testing procedure and results on the prototype
Items.Abstract: In the ELT, the wavefront correction is demanded to a quaternary deformable mirror; the M4 will be the largest DM ever built, with 5000+ actuators controlling its optical surface 2.5 m in diameter, segmented into 6 petals. Given its size, high actuator counts and tight operational requirements, it is mandatory for the optical calibration procedure to implement a large degree of automation, from initial alignment to system monitoring and to final reporting.  In this contribution, we summarize the procedure we developed for the LBT and VLT adaptive secondaries and fine tuned for the segmented M4; the focus will be on the actors, interfaces, data flow, data tracking, segments management and automation. The procedure, tested on the M4 Demonstration prototype, includes Optical Test Tower alignment, preliminary segments shaping, noise evaluation, measurement of Influence Functions and flattening in closed loop, calibration of the M4 metrology and phasing.

Items.Authors: Antonia Merdanevic Yáñez, Marilyn Cruces
Items.Title: Transformative sustainable solutions in radio astronomy: the FRONTIERS Project
Items.Abstract: Chile is a premier astronomical hub, yet the field lags in limiting carbon footprints, particularly in radio astronomy. FRONTIERS addresses this as a sustainable telescope prototype (UC Chile/Max-Planck), aiming for high-impact science with resource awareness. The system uses a "Small Diameter, Large Number" array to overcome manufacturing limits, optimized to ~25,000 EUR/element with uncooled components and local fabrication.    This work details the mechanical engineering of the 1–2 GHz parabolic antenna. The design features a hybrid Glass Fiber Reinforced Polymer (GFRP) structure on a Hot-Dip Galvanized A36 steel mount, with a metallized coating for reflectivity. Its modular, petal-based architecture facilitates local manufacturing and remote assembly. Validated by simulations, this design demonstrates that local technologies can ensure structural and electromagnetic performance while significantly reducing carbon footprints.

Items.Authors: Pascal Birckigt, Jonathan J. Carter, Gilbert Leibeling, Artem Basalaev, Johannes Lehmann, Carolin Rothhardt, Sina M. Koehlenbeck, Stefan Risse
Items.Title: Compact mechanical resonators for seismic isolation in gravitational wave observatories
Items.Abstract: The measurement of gravitational waves (GW) creates the most rigorous demands on seismic isolation of any experiment demonstrated today. Technological progress is required. We present a novel manufacturing method for compact, low resonance frequency, high-Q mechanical resonators. The key idea is fused silica wafer direct bonding combined with chemical-mechanical polishing, resulting in monolithic pieces that feature double-side-polished “springs” which are 100 µm thin while being several cm long. Combined with a homodyne quadrature interferometer (HoQI), we have created compact, extremely sensitive inertial sensors: Measurements in a GW detector prototype facility prove that our sensor’s displacement and acceleration noise – despite the resonator having a test mass of only 3 g – already matches that of bulky, kilogram-scale state-of-the-art sensors. Our work is relevant for next-gen GW observatories (Einstein telescope, Cosmic Explorer), atom interferometers and EUV lithography tools.

Items.Authors: Ben Buky, Cédric Taïssir Héritier, Fabio Rossi, Charlotte Z. Bond, Noah Schwartz, Guido Agapito, Juan Carlos Guerra, Enrico Pinna, Sam Ragland, Jean-François Sauvage
Items.Title: DM/WFS mis-registration tracking: implementation and on-sky validation of SPRINT at LBT
Items.Abstract: The advent of telescopes with an integrated deformable mirror (DM) presents new challenges for adaptive optics (AO) systems. The alignment between the DM and wavefront sensor (WFS) is expected to regularly evolve during operations due to their large separation. Without tracking and correction, these mis-registrations between the DM and WFS lead to loop instability, preventing diffraction limited performance from being realised. SPRINT, introduced in [Heritier et al, 2021], provides an approach to track these mis-registrations during observations. Rotation, shift, and magnification mis-registrations can all be recovered. The Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) has no current method for this, and SPRINT is also the baseline for the AO modes of the HARMONI instrument. We present an overview of SPRINT, and experimental results from on-sky testing at LBT to validate the method. Additionally, we report on the successful integration of SPRINT into the LBT real time computer.

Items.Authors: Beth Garton, Iain A. Steele, Helen E. Jermak, Chloe Miossec, Stuart D. Bates
Items.Title: On-sky rapid prototyping of the Squash spectrograph
Items.Abstract: The New Robotic Telescope (NRT) will be a 4-metre class fully autonomous telescope on La Palma. Its instrumentation suite builds on that of the Liverpool Telescope (LT) with a range of low-cost, reliable instruments that are easily maintained. Squash will be NRT’s flagship spectrograph; designed for the rapid classification of galactic and extragalactic transient and variable events. The LT, and its future partner facility the NRT, are autonomous telescopes with limited human access; these facilities require no-fuss instrumentation, which are all co-mounted at the telescope Cassegrain focus. Many of the current LT instrumentation suite are designed with moving parts; although these have proven to be reliable, the presence of moving parts makes failure more likely. Thus, to increase reliability and lower maintenance requirements, we have completed research and development for a low-resolution spectrograph with no moving parts.

Items.Authors: Adrian K. Sinclair, Chris Albert, C. Matt Bradford, Patrick Brown, Sean Bryan, Jesse Coldsmith, Jennifer Corekin, Sumit Dahal, Thomas K. Devlin, Thomas Essinger-Hileman, Logan Foote, Marc Foote, Draisy Friedman, Alessandro Geist, Jason Glenn, Christopher Green, Kyle Helson, Kevin Horgan, Tracee Jamison-Hooks, Elijah Kane, Jared Lucey, Philip Mauskopf, Lynn Miles, Sanetra Bailey Newman, Gerard Quilligan, Cody Roberson, Salman Sheikh, Manuel Vega, Eric Weeks, Christopher Wilson, Travis Wise
Items.Title: PRIMA prototype spaceflight KID readout electronics laboratory characterization
Items.Abstract: We present the development and testing of prototype kinetic inductance detector (KID) readout electronics for the PRobe far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA). PRIMA is a NASA Probe-class astrophysics mission concept with two science instruments, FIRESS and PRIMAger, which provide spectroscopic and polarimetric imaging from 24 to 261 um. We present measurements of the prototype readout coupled to prototype PRIMA/FIRESS detectors using a flight-like cryogenic RF chain with low-noise amplifiers at temperatures of 18K and 100K. We demonstrate cosmic ray pulse detection and real-time removal with an algorithm implemented in firmware. Finally, we discuss the crosstalk performance and investigate an optional dynamic range extension with multiple tones per resonance for viewing high contrast astrophysical scenes.

Items.Authors: Rachel E. Morgan, Eduardo Bendek, Carson Valdez, Anne Kroo, Kevin Fogarty, Rus Belikov, Jonathan Lin, David A.B. Miller, Olav Solgaard, Dan Sirbu
Items.Title: High contrast imaging with the AstroPIC integrated photonic coronagraph
Items.Abstract: Integrated photonics is a promising coronagraph technology option for increasing the Exo-Earth science yield of NASA’s Habitable Worlds Observatory and relaxing key observatory requirements. A photonic integrated circuit (PIC) coronagraph is theoretically capable of achieving extremely high performance because arrays of integrated interferometers can implement any optical transformation, including a near-optimal coronagraph. However, PIC coronagraphs require maturation before use in a space telescope mission. The AstroPIC project is advancing this technology by developing a proof-of-concept silicon-photonic PIC coronagraph in the near-infrared.     In this talk, we will review the design of AstroPIC and present results from laboratory testing of the first set of PIC devices fabricated for the project, including experiments that achieve over 90 dB extinction (<1e-9 contrast) of a single input channel and over 60 dB extinction (<1e-6 contrast) of multiple illuminated inputs.

Items.Authors: Emily Ronson, Robert J. Harris, Ariadna Calcines Rosario
Items.Title: Millimetre-scale spectrographs for next-generation photonic instrumentation
Items.Abstract: We present a set of ultra-compact spectrographs fabricated using two-photon polymerisation (2PP), each under 2.5 mm in length and printed directly onto an optical fibre. This fully integrated, alignment-free architecture enables extremely low-mass instrumentation with broad potential across astrophotonics, space systems, drone-based sensing, and quantum optics. Three configurations are presented; they combine beam-expansion optics, dispersive elements, and stray-light suppression within monolithic printed structures optimised for H-band operation. Coarse gratings provide resolving powers of approximately R ≈ 30. Experimental characterisation confirms the feasibility of fibre-coupled, fully printed spectrographs and demonstrates their promise as deployable components for next-generation integrated photonic instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Amira Bouikni, Mathias Nowak, Sylvestre Lacour, Jean-Tristan Buey, Elsa Huby, Jehanne Sarrazin, Luis Esteras Otal, Şenol Yazici, Samuel Lévêque, Mathis Houllé, Jules Scigliuto, Florentin Millour, Bruno Lopez
Items.Title: Advancing high-contrast interferometry for exoplanet detection and characterization
Items.Abstract: Long baseline optical interferometry now can probe astrophysical environments at angular separations beyond direct imaging, with GRAVITY and MATISSE enabling studies from young giant exoplanet atmospheres to compact circumstellar regions shaped by planet formation, accretion, and disk-planet interactions. However, high contrast interferometry remains limited by spectral artifacts, polarization dependent fringing, raw contrast leakage from residual aberrations, and strict phase stability requirements, as well as by the lack of reduction and analysis pipelines optimized for faint planetary signals across VLTI bands. To overcome these challenges on both instrumental and astrophysical aspects, we are developing new optical testbeds to improve beam combination, integrated optics, polarization control, and refined metrology, as well as engaging in collaborative initiatives to build next generation pipelines, including ExoMATISSE and future tools for upcoming high contrast instruments.

Items.Authors: Darshan A. Patel, Cody J. Duell
Items.Title: CCAT: readout power and frequency optimization of the 280 GHz instrument module Al and TiN KID arrays
Items.Abstract: The CCAT Observatory's Fred Young Submillimeter Telescope (FYST) is scheduled for deployment in 2026 with the Prime-Cam instrument. Prime-Cam will initially deploy with ~20,000 kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) in the 280 and 350 GHz instrument modules. KIDs are high quality factor resonating circuits that are read out by monitoring the complex transmission of a superposition of probe tones between 0.5 - 1 GHz. Accurately and efficiently tuning the powers and frequencies of the probe tones to optimize the performance of individual detectors is a challenging problem for large detector arrays. We use a variable temperature, cryogenic blackbody source inside a testbed receiver to measure the noise of the 280 GHz module TiN and Al KIDs, allowing us to develop a pipeline for optimizing their readout powers and frequencies. We present the current status of the tuning pipeline while highlighting differences between the TiN and Al KID tuning procedures.

Items.Authors: Nicholas M. Law, Hank Corbett, Alan Vasquez Soto, Alexandra Bucheli, Jonathan Carney, James Dockery, Megan Dubay, Shannon Fitton, Lawrence Machia, William Marshall, Thomas Procter, Michael Ronco, Donovan Schlekat, Glenn Walters
Items.Title: Exploring the deep high-speed sky with the Argus Array
Items.Abstract: The Argus Array is a new 8m-class optical survey telescope, under construction and planned for first light in 2027. Argus multiplexes 1200 small-aperture telescopes to form a 120-gigapixel survey system with 1” sampling over an 8,000-square-degree field of view, taking hundreds of images of each part of the sky each night. The Array will build a two-color, millions-of-epochs movie of the Northern sky, giving the astronomical community the remarkable ability to follow the evolution of every deep time-variable source -- simultaneously. Argus will be able to follow-up wide-area multiwavelength triggers orders of magnitude faster than current tiling astronomical surveys, monitor 100 million stars for planet-induced microlensing events, occultations, flares and other variability, and perform dozens of other surveys with data that will be made public on extremely rapid timescales. I will present the Array's status, unique design, and our path towards first light in 2027.

Items.Authors: Ross Cheriton, Suresh Sivanandam, Ernst de Mooij, Adam Densmore
Items.Title: Compact, high spatial and spectral resolution space-based integral field correlation spectrographs via massive astrophotonic multiplexing
Items.Abstract: Despite their scientific value, no space-based, high–spectral-resolution integral field spectrographs currently exist due to their prohibitive cost, size, and complexity. We propose a novel, highly multiplexed astrophotonic integral field spectrograph architecture that overcomes these barriers, enabling large-scale exoplanet atmosphere and biosignature surveys. The concept employs arrays of silicon nitride photonic chips with high-throughput, tunable cross-correlation filter arrays spanning the visible to short-wave infrared (H-band). This design simultaneously measures gas-specific transit curves and achieves high radial velocity precision at moderate spatial resolution, using polarization duplexing for enhanced information content.

Items.Authors: Thibaud Van Gorp, Pablo Roldán-Varona, Calum A. Ross, Christopher Evans, Aurélien Benoît, Duncan P. Hand, David Lee, Robert R. Thomson
Items.Title: Laser based manufacturing of freeform fused silica image slicers
Items.Abstract: Image slicers are key components in many astronomical instruments, notably in the VLT-MUSE instrument. However, the precision manufacturing of image slicers is costly and time-consuming. We present here a fully laser based method to manufacture precision fused silica image slicers. Individual slices are shaped with Ultrafast Laser-Assisted Etching at sub-µm level. A CO2 laser is used to post-process the optical surfaces and reduce the roughness Sq < 5 nm RMS without overall form alteration. The image slicer is assembled with passive alignment and coated with a 100 nm aluminium layer allowing a first optical characterisation mapping the reflected spots on a screen. This first prototype confirms that laser based manufacturing of freeform image slicers for astronomy is possible.

Items.Authors: Alan Davis, Lahiru Raffell, Luca Stringhetti, Randall Wayth, André van Es, Mark Waterson, Ivan Lloro
Items.Title: Low Noise Amplifier Reliability at the SKA-Low Site
Items.Abstract: The SKA-Low telescope presents some unique instrumentation challenges in radio astronomy. The telescope is situated in a remote, adverse desert climate in the outback of Western Australia and subject to natural prevailing weather patterns. The full SKA-Low telescope design necessitates the use of 262,144 low-noise amplifiers (LNA) that are situated at the apex of antennas and subject to the full range of environmental conditions at the site. Due to these factors, particularly the scale of the telescope and the remoteness of the site, reliability is of utmost importance. This paper will review the environmental conditions of the SKA-Low LNA hardware and identify a failure mode experienced in the SKA-Low LNAs on site in the first 4 stations constructed. Methods employed to identify LNA hardware failure modes via live bandpass characterisation will be presented along with detailed microelectronic analysis used to determine root cause and failure mechanisms in the LNA electronics.

Items.Authors: Hiroshi Matsuo, Hajime Ezawa, Tomohiro Koseki, Shotaro Inoue, Tetsusaburo Seino
Items.Title: Development of far-infrared intensity interferometry
Items.Abstract: For high angular resolution far-infrared (FIR) observations, space-borne interferometers have been studied. To realize long baseline and high sensitivity FIR observations, we work on intensity interferometry. By measuring fast intensity fluctuation from thermal sources, intensity correlations and delay time can be measured to obtain complex visibilities. We use SIS photon detectors and fast cryogenic readout electronics to measure intensity fluctuations. Our SIS photon detectors operate around 600 GHz and GaAs FETs are used for fast cryogenic readout electronics. We have realized high sensitivity measurement system for intensity fluctuation with a bandwidth of about 10 MHz. The performance is enough to measure intensity correlation in laboratory conditions. We will present our roadmap for Antarctic and space-borne intensity interferometry and their observational performance.

Items.Authors: Luca Rosignoli, Gabriele Rodeghiero, Sandrine Thomas, Guillem Megias Homar, Heejoo Choi, John Hill, Olga Kuhn, Elena Masciadri, Byeongjoon Jeong, Brandon Mechtley, Christian Veillet, Elana Urbach, Brian Stadler, Jason Chu, Alessio Taranto, Bryce Kalmbach, Joshua E. Meyers, Andrew J. Connolly, Rebekah Polen, John Franklin Crenshaw, Krzysztof Suberlak, Tiago Ribeiro, Roberto Tighe, Merlin Fisher-Levin, Mario Rivera, Enrico Giro, Rodolfo Canestrari, Holger Drass, Pablo Zorzi, Massimo Brescia
Items.Title: Laser-based metrology systems vs wavefront sensing techniques: a comparative overview between the Large Binocular Telescope and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory for the telescope alignment and collimation tracking
Items.Abstract: We present a comparative overview of the alignment strategies employed by the Large Binocular Telescope (LBT) and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory. Despite sharing an 8m aperture and fast focal ratios, they adopt reciprocal architectures. For initial alignment, LBT relies on Wavefront Sensing via Focal Plane Image Analysis, whereas Rubin aims to use a Laser Tracker to coarse align the telescope prior to closing the Active Optics System loop. Conversely, for maintaining collimation during observations, strategies reverse: LBT employs a laser-based Telescope Metrology System, while Rubin relies on the Curvature Wavefront Sensing using dedicated detectors at the focal plane corners. We analyze the strengths and trade-offs of these opposite philosophies. This study distills lessons learned to inform design strategies for future ELT instrumentation.

Items.Authors: Manny M. Montoya, Katie Morzinski, Amali Vaz, Oli Durney, Dan Vargas, Lauren Perez, Bianca Payan, Andrew Gardner, Jess Johnson, Suresh Sivanandam, Craig Kulesa, Ruby Huie, Hiram Olivas, Jarron Leisenring, Maggie Kautz, Krishna Kanuma, Jorge Sanchez, Saraswathi Subramanian, Orlando Trevino, Jenny Patience
Items.Title: MAPS, the MMT adaptive optics exoPlanet characterization system update
Items.Abstract: This update focuses on the Adaptive Secondary (AO) system on the MMT 6.5m telescope, which has been operating on-sky for the past four years. The review will cover the system’s performance, including the Adaptive Secondary, the Sapphira-fed IR Wavefront Sensor, the CACAO reconstructor, and the MIRAC imaging camera. Improvements aimed at reducing setup and ramp-up time at the start of AO observations will also be discussed, enabling future runs to require fewer engineering personnel. In addition, first-light results for the AO spectrograph ARIES in Spring 2026 will be presented, along with insights into the future direction of this project and the scientific opportunities ARIES will enable.

Items.Authors: Simon Tartakovsky, Steven J. Benton, William C. Jones
Items.Title: picoMUX: microcontroller based time-domain multiplexing readout for kilo-pixel TES arrays
Items.Abstract: Advances in SQUID based time-domain multiplexing (TDM) have outpaced their warm readout electronics. Next generation CMB telescopes are baselining kilo-pixel TES arrays with few viable electronic options. We present picoMUX, a new TDM readout electronics architecture that replaces the FPGA typically used in such systems, with a complement of modern microcontrollers. Designed around the current generation NIST multiplexer, it fully exploits its differential nature and two-level switching. The system achieves the required timing metrics (0.5 µs row dwell time and 50 MS/s sampling) while boasting drastic reductions in cost (≈$1/column), complexity, and power (≈0.1W/column) in the digital section over a comparable FPGA solution. Preliminary validation shows noise performance comparable to the MCE developed by UBC. picoMUX demonstrates how recent advances in microcontrollers enable simpler, low-power, low-cost TDM readouts for kilo-pixel TES arrays.

Items.Authors: Simon C. Ellis
Items.Title: Optimised sampling for astronomical instruments via compressed sensing
Items.Abstract: The conventional approach in astronomical instruments is to sample the signal at more than twice the Nyquist frequency; for example, the pixels in an imager are generally less than half the full-width half maximum of the point spread function, and in spectroscopy spectral pixels are less than half the full-width half maximum of the line spread function. This leads to a requirement for very large numbers of pixels in order to sample a wide-field image or a broad-band spectrum. However, recent developments in data science have shown that for certain types of signal, it is possible to significantly under-sample measurements and recover the full signal at high fidelty using a technique called compressed sensing. Here we describe this technique, and explore potential applications to the design of astronomical instruments with optimised sampling, including imaging, spectroscopy, integral field spectroscopy and wavefront sensing.

Items.Authors: Kieran S. O'Brien, Meryem K. Dag
Items.Title: SuperSMART: the superconducting spectrograph for medium resolution in an ARray of telescopes
Items.Abstract: SuperSMART is a novel concept for medium resolution optical and near-IR spectroscopy focussed on Time Domain Astronomy. It uses an array of commercial telescopes which each feed light independently via one or more fibers to a cryostat containing an array of Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detectors (MKIDs). This array forms a number of channels of a medium spectral resolution (R=5-10,000) wide passband (350-1800nm) spectrograph, using the KIDSpec concept (O'Brien, JLTP, 2020). The array of telescopes can either be pointed at different targets across the visible sky, or pointed at the same target and the light from each channel can be (incoherently) combined to form an equivalently larger aperture telescope. MKIDs are read-noise free, photon counting detectors this combining/stacking does not pay the read-noise penalty of semiconductor-based instruments. SuperSMART leverages the much improved cost/aperture of prosumer robotic telescopes, compared to standard 4-8m monolithic telescopes.

Items.Authors: Nico Deshler, Amit Ashok
Items.Title: Quantum limits of exoplanet discovery around resolved stars
Items.Abstract: We investigate the quantum limits of exoplanet detection and localization around partially resolved stars with finite angular extent. In this model, the density operator describing the state of the incoming optical field has an infinite-dimensional support over the Hilbert space of band-limited square-normalized spatial modes. Therefore, we numerically evaluate two fundamental quantum bounds: (1) The quantum Chernoff exponent which provides an asymptotic lower bound on the minimum achievable probability of error for exoplanet detection, (2) The quantum Cramer-Rao bound which provides a lower bound on the minimum achievable uncertainty for unbiased estimators of the exoplanet orbital position. We subsequently compare the performance of even-order coronagraphs against these bounds and propose a new quantum-optimal coronagraph which can accelerate the rate of exoplanet discovery over the domain of sub-diffraction orbits.

Items.Authors: Hariharan Krishnan, Mark Waterson, Andre van Es
Items.Title: SKA Low digital signal chain architecture and implementation

Items.Authors: Muskan Shinde, Isaac Bernardino Dinis, Nicolas Blind, Sylvain Cetre, Mary Angelie M. Alagao, Romain Fetick, Vincent Chambouleyron, Christophe Lovis, Nathanaël Restori, Benoît Neichel, Thierry Fusco, Bruno Chazelas
Items.Title: The near-infrared unmodulated pyramid wavefront sensor for RISTRETTO: First on-sky results at PAPYRUS bench
Items.Abstract: To meet the performance requirements of RISTRETTO instrument high sensitivity to low-order wavefront aberrations is essential. The Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (PWFS), known for its high sensitivity, is therefore a strong candidate. However, the PWFS has non-linearities and a limited dynamic range. The classical solution of applying modulation to increase this range reduces sensitivity and AO system speed. To overcome these limitations, we propose using an unmodulated PWFS in the near-infrared (NIR-uPWFS), since the dynamic range increases linearly with wavelength. This removes the need for modulation and its associated drawbacks. We tested the NIR-uPWFS on the PAPYRUS bench at OHP. The new pyramid was installed on the IR arm of the bench, which already hosted a modulated PWFS in the visible (VIS-mPWFS). The NIR-uPWFS successfully closed the AO loop with a simple integrator and linear reconstructor. On average, the NIR-uPWFS provided a Strehl ratio 1.60 times higher than the VIS-mPWFS.

Items.Authors: Kevin A. Bundy, Matthew DeMartino, Jordan Diaz, Rebecca Jensen-Clem, Aditya Sengupta, Pradip Gatkine, Stephanie Sallum, Avi Patel, Holger Schmidt, Michael Fitzgerald, Elinor Gates, Stephen Eikenberry, Dylan Brocchini-Rose, Anna Gagnebin
Items.Title: The APALO testbed: advancing astrophotonics at Lick Observatory
Items.Abstract: Astrophotonic technologies provide exciting opportunities to sense and manipulate light in new ways, opening paths to miniaturized, stable, and less expensive instrumentation. As these technologies mature, it is increasingly important to test them on a telescope to retire risk and develop experience building cost-effective, scientifically productive astrophotonic instrumentation. This is the motivation behind APALO (Astrophotonics Advancement at Lick Observatory), a new, dedicated astrophotonics testbed behind the AO system at Lick Observatory's 3m Shane Telescope. Here we describe the design and commissioning of APALO as well as initial on-sky characterization and testing with photonic lanterns and chip-based devices. As a facility instrument, APALO is a community resource of UC Observatories. We welcome and encourage collaboration with astrophotonic and instrumentation groups worldwide.

Items.Authors: Adrian M. Glauser, Sascha P. Quanz, Christina Agyemang, Felix A. Dannert, Maximilian Kirchhoff, Judy Lai-Norling, Eleonora Alei, Thomas Birbacher, Joost A. van den Born, Dennis Dolkens, David Eglin, Jérôme Faist, Andrea Fortier, Germain Garreau, Rachel Grange, Jonah T. Hansen, Philipp A. Huber, Robert Huisman, Michael J. Ireland, Jens Kammerer, Kevin Kouwenhoven, Romain Laugier, Tim Lichtenberg, Oliver Pitz, Eckhart Spalding, Floris van der Tak, Pieter de Visser
Items.Title: The Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE): establishing the foundations for a space-based exoplanet interferometer
Items.Abstract: The Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) is a proposed space mission designed to spectrally characterize the thermal emission of temperate, terrestrial exoplanets in the solar neighbourhood. Its ultimate goal is to assess the prevalence of life capable of producing global atmospheric biosignatures on these worlds. LIFE employs a formation-flying nulling interferometer operating in the mid-infrared wavelength range.  The mission is currently in an early definition phase, with a full concept study now ramping up. In preparation for this study, we have conducted a series of targeted pre-studies to help define the mission scope and explore the relevant trade space. In this presentation, we will outline the current status and programmatic approach of the mission definition and feasibility assessment, introduce the updated reference concept, and report on ongoing and required technology development activities.

Items.Authors: Andrea Chiodini, Fallon Konow, Daniele Calchetti, Dario Del Moro, Luca Giovannelli, Stuart Mark Jefferies, Neil Murphy, Ermanno Pietropaolo, Vincenzo Rizi, Wayne Rodgers, Giorgio Viavattene, Emanuele Avocone, Francesco Berrilli
Items.Title: The new and improved TSST: advancing toward a robotic solar facility for continuous space weather monitoring
Items.Abstract: To support continuous space weather monitoring, the Tor Vergata Synoptic Solar Telescope (TSST) employs a Magneto-Optical Filter (MOF) channel capable of providing simultaneous line-of-sight full-disk velocity and magnetic field maps of the solar photosphere and an Halpha channel for complementary chromospheric imaging and flare detection. Both channels of the TSST will be integrated into a robotic dome, enabling the TSST to operate as an autonomous facility for continuous space weather monitoring. We present the final optomechanical assembly along with results from test observations.

Items.Authors: Eliza Gazda
Items.Title: Tone-tracking readout demonstration on kinetic inductance detectors
Items.Abstract: Microwave observatories require an ever-increasing number of superconducting detectors, demanding a readout solution that can fully harness the sensitivity of large focal planes. Kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) offer high sensitivity and natural multiplexing, but their performance degrades when fixed probe tones become detuned under varying optical loading. Such detuning leads to excess noise, unstable responsivity, and operational overhead from manual retuning. We present the performance of a tone-tracking readout for KIDs under variable optical loading from a cold load. The system is implemented on a Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC) platform running SLAC Microresonator Radio Frequency (SMuRF) firmware. We measure detector noise and responsivity and compare these results to a fixed-tone readout. Our readout system enables peak detector sensitivity and reduces operational overhead for large-format KID arrays used in ongoing and future astronomy and cosmology experiments.

Items.Authors: Meryem Kubra Dag, Kieran O'Brien, Simone Scaringi, James Gill-Fleming, Isabelle Crossley
Items.Title: KIDSpec: a photon-counting spectrograph for time-domain astronomy
Items.Abstract: KIDSpec is a medium-resolution UVOIR echelle spectrograph concept that uses optical and near-IR MKID arrays. MKIDs are superconducting photon-counting detectors that record individual photons with microsecond timing and estimate their energies. Using this intrinsic energy resolution, KIDSpec separates echelle orders directly in the detector readout, removing the need for cross-disperser optics and improving throughput. The photon-based stream is immune to dark current and enables rapid rejection of cosmic-ray events, giving KIDSpec a clear advantage over CCD/CMOS systems. In this presentation, we outline the KIDSpec concept, show simulations for different telescope sizes, and present initial prototype results.

Items.Authors: Johan Mazoyer, María Jesús Mellado Tenorio, Axel Potier, Christian Wilkinson, Pierre Baudoz, Raphaël Galicher, Iva Laginja, Lukas Delaye
Items.Title: Coherence differential imaging using random forest regression for the direct detection of exoplanets
Items.Abstract: Coronagraphic imaging of exoplanets is limited by residual speckles that mimic planets. Advanced post-processing is essential for current and future instruments on the ground or in space.  Current techniques are time-intensive and limited. ADI requires long sequences and is limited at small separation. RDI is also time-consuming and sensitive to speckle evolution, leading to imperfect subtraction. Coherence Differential Imaging (CDI) offers a faster alternative by using the light incoherence between speckles and planets, but its reliance on accurate instrumental models limits performance.  After demonstration on SPHERE, we enhanced CDI with a Random Forest algorithm. This method models the differential signal as a high-dimensional regression problem, optimizing the discrimination between coherent speckle noise and the incoherent planet signal. We validate this enhanced CDI using testbed data reproducing Roman CGI conditions.

Items.Authors: Karolina Kubiak, Robert Ligon, Rainer Köhler, Theo ten Brummelaar, Gail Schaefer, Douglas R. Gies, Narsireddy Anugu, Nic Scott, Christopher Farrington
Items.Title: Control, calibration, and performance of the twelve adaptive optics systems at the CHARA Array
Items.Abstract: We describe the engineering implementation of CHARA’s twelve AO systems—six telescope AO units and six laboratory AO units. LabAO provides calibration and static aberration control, while TelAO performs high-speed atmospheric correction. A shared telemetry and control framework links all twelve systems. On-sky use shows improved image quality, improved fringe contrast, and reduced differential aberrations across beams.

Items.Authors: Daniel van der Schuur, Gijs Schoonderbeek, Ágnes Mika, Roel Witvers, Paula Fusiara, Lesley Goudbeek
Items.Title: Ethernet Receiver: synchronized antennas with ethernet connectivity
Items.Abstract: The Ethernet Receiver is a novel FPGA-based platform developed at ASTRON, the Netherlands Institute for Radio Astronomy, addressing the demanding requirements of next-generation radio telescopes. Designed to replace traditional coaxial signal transport with high-speed optical fibre interconnects, the platform integrates synchronized analog-to-digital conversion (ADC) close to the antenna, transmitting both clock references and digitized data over Ethernet.     In this presentation, we will describe two Ethernet Receiver platforms currently under development: a low-band variant (EthRx-L) and a high-band variant (EthRx-H). Both platforms employ White Rabbit technology to achieve precision timing.

Items.Authors: Sebin Sebastian Xavier, Guillermo Martin, Simon Gross
Items.Title: Towards an integrated optic beam combiner fabricated using ultrafast laser inscription for the SUBARU/FIRST Instrument
Items.Abstract: Study on the development of an integrated optic beam combiner to be used at the SUBARU telescope in the FIRST instrument as a recombination platform. The fabrication method used to develop such a chip is Ultrafast laser inscription or Femtosecond laser direct write. It enables one to fabricate wave guiding circuits in 3 Dimensions in the bulk of glass making it a very desirable technique to be used for the fabrication of a device that has good transmittance in the 600 to 900 nm spectral band. The fabricated device is a photonic beam combiner that will combine light form multiple subapertures of the telescope to produce an interferogram for the high contrast imaging of exoplanets.

Items.Authors: Kimi Spirig, Philipp A. Huber, Felix A. Dannert, Adrian M. Glauser, Sascha P. Quanz
Items.Title: Constraining planetary orbital parameters with the Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE)
Items.Abstract: The Large Interferometer For Exoplanets (LIFE) is a planned space-based nulling interferometer designed to directly detect and characterize temperate, terrestrial exoplanets in the Solar neighborhood. Unlike classical imaging instruments, LIFE does not record spatially resolved images but instead its observable is a time-domain signal. Data reduction therefore relies on matching the data with pre-calculated templates that depend on the planetary position. Previous studies have assumed planets to remain static with respect to their host stars during an observation, an approximation that breaks down in certain scenarios like the observation of habitable-zone planets around M-dwarfs.  We present first work on the impact of planetary orbital motion on data reduction and means to address it. We further investigate LIFE's ability to constrain the orbital parameters from single observations as a function of integration time, a factor relevant for mission scheduling and instrument definition.

Items.Authors: Abarna Karthikeyan, Tracee Jamison-Hooks, Oketa Basha, Sean Bryan, Philip Mauskopf, Lynn Miles, Sanetra Newman-Bailey, Adrian Sinclair, Thomas Essinger-Hileman
Items.Title: Evolving architectures in space-qualified signal processing readout electronics for HabWorlds and origins detector systems
Items.Abstract: Future space observatories spanning optical, near-infrared, and far-infrared wavelengths, including the Habitable  Worlds Observatory (HWO) and the Probe Far-Infrared Mission for Astrophysics (PRIMA), require scalable,  spaceflight-oriented digital readout architectures capable of supporting large-format Microwave Kinetic Inductance Detector (MKID) arrays operating across multi-gigasample-per-second bandwidths.  This paper presents continuing architectural developments from the collaborative NASA GSFC and Arizona  State University (ASU) SESE MKID readout effort supporting technologies relevant to future HWO-class de-  tector systems. The work represents a collaborative technology maturation pathway between NASA engineering  teams and ASU focused on the development of deterministic, flight-reviewable Field Programmable Gate Array  (FPGA) signal-processing architectures for next-generation astrophysics missions.

Items.Authors: Clark E. Baker, John S. Young, Martin Fisher, Samantha J. Thompson, Eugene Seneta, Alireza Esmaeilzadeh, Didier Queloz, Peter Pedersen, Tim Naylor, Ian Wellaway, Jay Fitzpatrick, Tomáš Turek, Martin Šulc, Petr Kačer, Alberto Madrigal Aguado, Andrew W. Ridings, Carlos Martín Perez, Cecilia Fariña, Chris Benn, Don Abrams, Eduardo Mantero, Frank Gribbin, Joel Concepción, Judith Santos-Torres, Jure Skvarc, Kevin Dee, Lara Monteagudo, Lucía Suárez-Andrés, Luis Hernández, Marc Balcells, Nada Ihanec, Neil O'Mahony, Roberto Martínez, Rubén Sánchez Janssen
Items.Title: The roboticisation of the Isaac Newton Telescope: the largest robotic telescope in the world
Items.Abstract: In this publication, we are happy to announce the successful roboticization of the 2.54m Isaac Newton Telescope (INT). The INT has been thoroughly refurbished and serviced; this includes: new motors and encoders for the telescope, dome and shutters, a meteorological weather station with an extensive suite of sensors, a complete telescope control system which interacts with instrumentation control software, and a series of safety systems for both equipment and personnel. The robust, reliable and accurate core mechanical ‘bones’ and optics of the INT remain. This comprehensive overhaul brings the INT to modern standards and enables it to operate completely autonomously. Great effort has been made to maximise the reliability of the system, with long mean time to failure and low mean time to repair. It is foreseen that this upgrade will enable the INT to operate efficiently and effectively for many decades to come.

Items.Authors: Takeshi Nakamori, Mana Hasebe, Miu Maeshiro, Hiroto Sasaki, Anju Sato, Tomohiro Sato, Kazuaki Hashiyama, Masayoshi Shoji, Ryotaro Honda, Masaya Miyahara, Koji S. Kawabata, Tatsuya Nakaoka, Masaru Kino, Kazuhiro Takefuji, Hiroaki Misawa, Kotaro Niinuma, Dai Takei
Items.Title: Development of a high-time-resolution optical photon-counting instrument IMONY for fast transient astronomy
Items.Abstract: IMONY is a high-time-resolution optical photon-counting instrument designed for the study of fast optical transients, including coherent or rapidly varying emission from compact objects. The system records individual photons with 100-ns timing accuracy using a 64-pixel Geiger-mode APD array and FPGA-based readout, enabling unbinned analysis and simultaneous optical–radio timing. IMONY has been deployed on ground-based telescopes, demonstrating stable performance in extended campaigns. A newly developed version, incorporating high-integration analog ASICs and a compact modular detector unit, further expands its applicability to multi-wavelength and time-domain astronomy.

Items.Authors: Simon Carrier, Jean-Pierre Véran, Maaike van Kooten, Kate Jackson, Jean-François Pratte, Serge Charlebois
Items.Title: Time-resolved pyramid wavefront sensor experimental results on REVOLT AO bench
Items.Abstract: Pyramid wavefront sensors (PWFS) offer excellent sensitivity, but suffer from non-linear behavior. This is typically mitigated by modulating the guide star image around the pyramid’s apex, which improves linearity but reduces sensitivity.    We are developing a Time-Resolved Pyramid Wavefront Sensor (TR-PWFS) that leverages the high temporal resolution of our SPAD-based detectors to break the modulation cycle into discrete time frames. By processing these frames individually, we improve robustness to detector noise and get higher AO performance.    In this paper, we will present on-sky results of the TR-PWFS on the PWFS arm of the REVOLT AO bench using a commercial SPAD-based camera with the aim of running 500Hz. In addition, we will report simulation results showing how the TR-PWFS offers advantages compared to the typical modulated and unmodulated PWFS for NPCAs and petaling errors in segmented-pupil systems.

Items.Authors: Babak N. Saif, Breann N. Sitarski, Johannes Borregaard, Aleksandr Mokeev
Items.Title: Fundamental limits of classical high contrast imaging and new opportunities through quantum enhanced optical processing
Items.Abstract: Coherent starlight suppression techniques are tools for enabling direct observations of faint companions near bright stars. These methods are constrained by several fundamental considerations . We discuss these limits in a unified way. One limit is set by spatial coherence. The planet and the star electric fields overlap slightly at the entrance pupil. A coronagraph suppresses the part of the star orthogonal to the planet field, but any shared component cannot be removed without suppressing the planet. This sets a floor that cannot be eliminated by coherent subtraction. Further, nulling the star at one wavelength does not null it at other wavelengths, but a broader bandwidth improves the photon statistics for field estimation. These effects define the true performance limits for any classical coronagraph combined with coherent subtraction. We describe how recent proposals including quantum enhanced optical imaging relate to these fundamental limits and provide new opportunities.

Items.Authors: Majd Mayyasi, Emil Atz, Patrick Lierle, John Clarke, Brian Walsh, Oswald Siegmund, Adrian Martin
Items.Title: High-resolution spectrograph at Lyman-a (HIRSL): an innovative optical design for high dispersion UV spectroscopy
Items.Abstract: A high-heritage echelle UV spectrograph has been redesigned in a compact space-deployable package while achieving equal or better spectral resolution, sensitivity, and maintaining low power consumption and low mass. The system is designed to measure UV emissions such as H & D Lyman-a, and O-triplet with <10 km/s resolution. The resulting spectral resolution surpasses state-of-the-art systems and enables unprecedented discovery of the different populations of H atoms that make up interplanetary hydrogen to better understand the dynamics at the edge of our Solar System – a key objective of the planned NASA Interstellar Probe (ISP) mission. Furthermore, this instrument has versatile applications for terrestrial, planetary, and cometary science that can complement lunar and planetary, as well as heliospheric missions.

Items.Authors: Olivier Perdereau, Reza Ansari, Antoine Back, Daniel Charlet, Cedric Esnault, Hadrien Grasland, Monique Taurigna, Paul-Eric Pottie, Cédric Dumez-Viou
Items.Title: IDROGEN boards on-sky qualification with the PAON4 radio interferometer
Items.Abstract: PAON4 is a 4 dishes radio interferometer installed at the Nancay Radio Observatory. This small array is devoted at demonstrating the effectiveness of data-taking, observing strategy and data analysis techniques for low-z (Z<.6) cosmology with the 21cm intensity mapping, using a large, compact array observing in transit mode. After a first phase ended in 2019, its acquisition system is now being upgraded with Idrogen boards. These generic digital electronics boards built around an Altera FPGA implement the white Rabbit timing system. They are complemented in our application by FMC mezzanine boards with 2 channel 1Gsamples/s ADCs. I'll review the in-lab tests we made to check the performances of the system, in particular the timing accuracy and stability, in which we observed am excellent stability and accuracy (within ~+/- 5ps peak to peak, over more than 50h). I'll show some technical details of their installation in the PAON4 system, and results from the first on sky observations.

Items.Authors: Maclean Rouble, Michel Adamic, Matt Dobbs, Joshua Montgomery, Ketan Sand, Sofiia Savchyn, Graeme Smecher
Items.Title: A kilo-pixel array of microwave kinetic inductance detectors operated with electro-quasiparticle feedback
Items.Abstract: As the technological readiness of microwave kinetic inductance detectors (KIDs) advances, a major opportunity for progress towards achieving instrument-level background-limited performance lies in the manner in which arrays of these detectors are operated. We have previously demonstrated an in-situ technique to address limitations encountered when operating highly multiplexed arrays by altering and maintaining the resonant frequency of individual KIDs under changing loads using fast, active, electro-quasiparticle feedback. This is implemented as a control loop which digitally modulates the readout current to feed back directly on the quasiparticle and supercurrent systems of the KID to guarantee optimal biasing, maintain spectral purity, and eliminate operational inter-resonator collisions.  We present results from the first use of this technique at deployment scale using a kilo-pixel KID array, and discuss its implications for effective array yield, responsivity, linearity, and noise.

Items.Authors: Matthijs Mars, Sebastiaan Y. Haffert, Jared R. Males, Joseph D. Long, Laird M. Close, Kyle Van Gorkom, Olivier Guyon, Alexander Hedglen, Parker T. Johnson, Maggie Y. Kautz, Jay K. Kueny, Rico Landman, Joshua Liberman, Miles Lucas, Jennifer Lumbres, Eden A. McEwen, Avalon McLeod, Tiffany Nguyen, Logan A. Pearce, Lauren Schatz, Elena Tonucci, Katie Twitchell, Alycia J. Weinberger
Items.Title: Non-linear low-order wavefront control with a physics-based digital twin: on-sky results from MagAO-X
Items.Abstract: We present a fully physics-based, differentiable digital twin of the focal-plane low-order wavefront sensor (FLOWFS) system on MagAO-X. This optical model enables both non-linear reconstruction of low-order aberrations and the derivation of a linear interaction matrix for high-speed (8 kHz) low-order control on-sky. By maintaining a stable wavefront at the coronagraph, we reduce stellar leakage and improve coronagraphic performance. Because the model is fully physics-based, it remains robust across changing observing conditions and transitions cleanly from laboratory to on-sky operation. It can also be rapidly adapted to different filters or coronagraph masks with minimal recalibration.

Items.Authors: Sagi Ben-Ami, Eran O. Ofek, Ofer Yaron, Oren Ironi, Yahel Sofer-Rimalt, Arie Blumenzweig, Daniel Golod, David Polishook, Hanindyo Kuncarayakti, Seppo Mattila, Tsevi Mazeh
Items.Title: The Multi-Aperture Spectroscopic Telescope: a novel telescope array at the Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory
Items.Abstract: The Multi-Aperture Spectroscopic Telescope (MAST) is a new, fiber-fed spectroscopic facility for the Weizmann Astrophysical Observatory in the Negev Desert, Israel. MAST is composed of 20 60cm F/3 prime-focus PlaneWave Instruments telescopes, operating as a flexible, cost-effective alternative to a single 3 m-class aperture. Each telescope feeds science and sky fibers through a custom coupling unit into a centralized 45-fiber quasi-slit that supports independent or combined observations. Two instruments deliver complementary capabilities: DeepSpec, a low-resolution broadband spectrograph for time-domain follow-up and object classification, and HighSpec, a high-resolution narrow-band spectrograph optimized for stellar, white dwarf, and ISM studies. MAST, currently in advanced commissioning phase, is designed for full robotic operation, fast target acquisition, and flexible scheduling, enabling efficient transient classification, stellar spectroscopy, wide surveys
